This Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) scientist was performing one of the last steps in a poliovirus testing process. Dyes are used to determine, which of the nucleotides (basis of genetic material) are present in a sequence. The outer coat of the virus (the capsid) is sequenced to find out where the virus has circulated. This machine is a sequencing instrument, a Sanger sequencer. Sanger sequencing implements a traditional type of sequencing. The plates go in, and the machine analyzes the reactions. Each base has a different color. The machine processes the bases, and sorts them, producing a chromatogram of four colors. See PHIL 22909 for an example of this four-color chromatogram. Sequencing gives CDC a window to where a virus has been, and how long it has been circulating. This allows CDC to focus our vaccination programs on specific regions inside pertinent countries.

<p>Global wastewater could produce over 800,000 GWh of chemical energy annually, and this is currently largely untapped.</p>
<p>The recovery of ammonia and phosphate using METs offers a compelling route to circular nutrient management and sustainable agriculture.</p>
<p>Despite promising lab-scale results, METs face challenges in scalability, energy efficiency, and cost, with pilot-scale systems often underperforming due to increased resistance and complex wastewater matrices.</p>
<p>Integrating METs with established treatment systems (e.g., anaerobic digestion or membrane bioreactors) and novel applications (e.g., hydroponics or remote sensors) extends their viability for both centralized and decentralized sanitation solutions.</p>
<p>Field deployments in underserved regions demonstrate the potential of METs for low-cost, decentralized energy and sanitation infrastructure, addressing multiple Sustainable Development Goals.</p>

cycles",["Date","2026-01-27T09:17:30.000Z"],["Date","2025-08-19T12:12:54.000Z"],["Date","2026-02-24T00:00:00.000Z"],["Date","2026-09-13T02:14:10.923Z"],"Global wastewater production exceeds 359 billion m3 annually, of which only 52% is treated, mostly in expensive and resource-consuming processes. Microbial electrochemical technologies (METs) offer a transformative approach to sustainable wastewater management by converting waste into valuable resources such as energy, clean water, and nutrients. They present a viable solution to the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 6 (to ensure access to water and sanitation for all) by enhancing both sanitation and resource recovery. METs, including microbial fuel cells (MFCs) and microbial electrolysis cells (MECs), harness electrogenic microorganisms to oxidize organic matter, generating electric energy or producing energy carriers like hydrogen and methane. METs also enable recovery of nutrients, such as ammonium and phosphates, which are essential for agriculture, thereby closing resource loops in a circular economy. Despite their potential, challenges remain in scaling up METs for widespread application. Pilot-scale MFCs and MECs have demonstrated feasibility, achieving up to 90% chemical oxygen demand removal and producing electric power, methane, or hydrogen from wastewater. However, high capital costs, material limitations, and energy efficiency barriers hinder commercialization. Innovations in electrode design, modular configurations, and integration with existing wastewater treatment processes (e.g., anaerobic digestion, membrane bioreactors, or constructed wetlands) are advancing METs toward higher technology readiness levels (TRLs 4–8). Field applications, like a system for urine-based electricity generation in underserved regions, highlight METs adaptability and societal impact. The transition from laboratory to real-world implementation requires scaling, process integration, and further optimization to reduce costs and improve performance. By aligning with circular economy principles, METs can transform wastewater into a resource, contributing to energy security, environmental sustainability, and global sanitation goals. ",{"data":1228,"content":1229,"nodeType":1133},{},[1230],{"data":1231,"marks":1232,"value":1233,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Wastewater contains three main resource pools:  ",{"data":1235,"content":1236,"nodeType":1284},{},[1237,1254,1269],{"data":1238,"content":1239,"nodeType":1253},{},[1240],{"data":1241,"content":1242,"nodeType":1133},{},[1243,1249],{"data":1244,"marks":1245,"value":1248,"nodeType":1124},{},[1246],{"type":1247},"bold","energy:",{"data":1250,"marks":1251,"value":1252,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," the organic matter in global wastewater holds over 800,000 GWh of energy each year","list-item",{"data":1255,"content":1256,"nodeType":1253},{},[1257],{"data":1258,"content":1259,"nodeType":1133},{},[1260,1265],{"data":1261,"marks":1262,"value":1264,"nodeType":1124},{},[1263],{"type":1247},"fertilizer nutrients:",{"data":1266,"marks":1267,"value":1268,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," around 14 million tons of nitrogen and about 3 million tons of phosphorus annually—equivalent to roughly 10–11% of global ammonia demand and around 7% of phosphate demand",{"data":1270,"content":1271,"nodeType":1253},{},[1272],{"data":1273,"content":1274,"nodeType":1133},{},[1275,1280],{"data":1276,"marks":1277,"value":1279,"nodeType":1124},{},[1278],{"type":1247},"water: ",{"data":1281,"marks":1282,"value":1283,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"after treatment, wastewater becomes clean water for irrigation, construction, industrial cooling, landscaping, and groundwater recharge—With further treatment it can become potable.","unordered-list",{"data":1286,"content":1287,"nodeType":1133},{},[1288],{"data":1289,"marks":1290,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1292,"content":1293,"nodeType":1133},{},[1294],{"data":1295,"marks":1296,"value":1297,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"These resources are currently removed or discarded separately, often at high energy cost.  ",{"data":1299,"content":1300,"nodeType":1133},{},[1301],{"data":1302,"marks":1303,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1305,"content":1306,"nodeType":1193},{},[1307],{"data":1308,"marks":1309,"value":1310,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"What are microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)? ",{"data":1312,"content":1313,"nodeType":1133},{},[1314],{"data":1315,"marks":1316,"value":1317,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Reclaiming these lost resources from wastewater can support cleaner water with lower net energy demand than current approaches.  ",{"data":1319,"content":1320,"nodeType":1133},{},[1321],{"data":1322,"marks":1323,"value":1324,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"\n\nThe authors discuss how METs—devices where special \"electrogenic” bacteria move electrons to electrodes as they digest waste—can help us achieve this. ",{"data":1326,"content":1327,"nodeType":1133},{},[1328],{"data":1329,"marks":1330,"value":1331,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"\n\nThe authors review two key types of MET:",{"data":1333,"content":1334,"nodeType":1284},{},[1335,1350],{"data":1336,"content":1337,"nodeType":1253},{},[1338],{"data":1339,"content":1340,"nodeType":1133},{},[1341,1346],{"data":1342,"marks":1343,"value":1345,"nodeType":1124},{},[1344],{"type":1247},"microbial fuel cells (MFCs):",{"data":1347,"marks":1348,"value":1349,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," these use electroactive microbes to oxidize organic matter at an anode and produce a small electrical current while the water is treated",{"data":1351,"content":1352,"nodeType":1253},{},[1353],{"data":1354,"content":1355,"nodeType":1133},{},[1356,1361],{"data":1357,"marks":1358,"value":1360,"nodeType":1124},{},[1359],{"type":1247},"microbial electrolysis cells (MECs):",{"data":1362,"marks":1363,"value":1364,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," these add some voltage so the cathode makes hydrogen (or sometimes methane) during treatment.",{"data":1366,"content":1367,"nodeType":1133},{},[1368],{"data":1369,"marks":1370,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1372,"content":1373,"nodeType":1193},{},[1374],{"data":1375,"marks":1376,"value":1377,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"What have pilot studies shown outside the lab? ",{"data":1379,"content":1380,"nodeType":1133},{},[1381],{"data":1382,"marks":1383,"value":1384,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Pilot projects show that METs can treat varying amounts of real wastewater. These range from tens of liters up to full-scale constructed wetlands, generally removing a substantial share of organics and nutrients. ",{"data":1386,"content":1387,"nodeType":1133},{},[1388],{"data":1389,"marks":1390,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1392,"content":1393,"nodeType":1133},{},[1394],{"data":1395,"marks":1396,"value":1397,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Schröder et al. classify the following examples using technology readiness levels (TRLs)—a standard scale for how close a technology is to real-world use, from 1 (least ready) to 9 (most ready): ",{"data":1399,"content":1400,"nodeType":1284},{},[1401,1416,1431,1446,1461,1476],{"data":1402,"content":1403,"nodeType":1253},{},[1404],{"data":1405,"content":1406,"nodeType":1133},{},[1407,1412],{"data":1408,"marks":1409,"value":1411,"nodeType":1124},{},[1410],{"type":1247},"constructed wetlands with MET media (METland®) ",{"data":1413,"marks":1414,"value":1415,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"in Europe that clean municipal and industrial wastewater (TRL 7–8) ",{"data":1417,"content":1418,"nodeType":1253},{},[1419],{"data":1420,"content":1421,"nodeType":1133},{},[1422,1427],{"data":1423,"marks":1424,"value":1426,"nodeType":1124},{},[1425],{"type":1247},"MFC-based biosensors",{"data":1428,"marks":1429,"value":1430,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," that monitor treatment performance and toxicity. Commercial systems use pre-loaded electrodes to give continuous signals linked to biological activity (TRL 6-9) ",{"data":1432,"content":1433,"nodeType":1253},{},[1434],{"data":1435,"content":1436,"nodeType":1133},{},[1437,1442],{"data":1438,"marks":1439,"value":1441,"nodeType":1124},{},[1440],{"type":1247},"modular MFC units for very concentrated industrial wastewater",{"data":1443,"marks":1444,"value":1445,"nodeType":1124},{},[],", which treat swine and beverage wastewaters continuously for months, removing organic pollution and generating some electricity (TRL 5-7) ",{"data":1447,"content":1448,"nodeType":1253},{},[1449],{"data":1450,"content":1451,"nodeType":1133},{},[1452,1457],{"data":1453,"marks":1454,"value":1456,"nodeType":1124},{},[1455],{"type":1247},"urine-focused MET stacks (Pee Power® and ammonia recovery)",{"data":1458,"marks":1459,"value":1460,"nodeType":1124},{},[]," that have powered toilet lighting at the UK’s Glastonbury Festival and in field trials in Uganda, Kenya, and South Africa. Scaled-up MECs have also recovered ammonia and phosphorus from source-separated urine (TRL 5-6) ",{"data":1462,"content":1463,"nodeType":1253},{},[1464],{"data":1465,"content":1466,"nodeType":1133},{},[1467,1472],{"data":1468,"marks":1469,"value":1471,"nodeType":1124},{},[1470],{"type":1247},"MFCs for municipal wastewater",{"data":1473,"marks":1474,"value":1475,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"—reactors of about 255–850 L that run for a year or more on real sewage. These operate reliably to remove a substantial amount of organic pollution, but produce far less electricity than equivalent lab systems (TRL 5-6) ",{"data":1477,"content":1478,"nodeType":1253},{},[1479],{"data":1480,"content":1481,"nodeType":1133},{},[1482,1487],{"data":1483,"marks":1484,"value":1486,"nodeType":1124},{},[1485],{"type":1247},"MECs for hydrogen and final treatment",{"data":1488,"marks":1489,"value":1490,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"—reactors of about 100–1,000 L at treatment plants and industrial sites such as winery and hydrothermal liquefaction wastewaters. ",{"data":1505,"content":1506,"nodeType":1133},{},[1507],{"data":1508,"marks":1509,"value":1510,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"In these scenarios, METs are added as extra steps in existing plants rather than replacing whole works. They are placed where wastewater is still relatively concentrated—early in the process or on side-streams from sludge handling and anaerobic digestion. This means they can recover organics and nutrients and reduce the load on later, more energy-intensive stages. ",{"data":1512,"content":1513,"nodeType":1133},{},[1514],{"data":1515,"marks":1516,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1518,"content":1519,"nodeType":1133},{},[1520],{"data":1521,"marks":1522,"value":1523,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Some systems are built directly into existing units (for example, into beds, tanks, or filters) so they can provide both treatment and recovery in the same footprint. Related bioelectrochemical systems can also be used purely as sensors, sitting in pipes or tanks and sending continuous performance markers, without changing the main processes. ",{"data":1525,"content":1526,"nodeType":1133},{},[1527],{"data":1528,"marks":1529,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1531,"content":1535,"nodeType":1179},{"target":1532},{"sys":1533},{"id":1534,"type":254,"linkType":1177},"ax9galbI1WWuPGgrwNcfC",[],{"data":1537,"content":1538,"nodeType":1133},{},[1539],{"data":1540,"marks":1541,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1543,"content":1544,"nodeType":1193},{},[1545],{"data":1546,"marks":1547,"value":1548,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"What are the current limits, and how can they be overcome? ",{"data":1550,"content":1551,"nodeType":1133},{},[1552],{"data":1553,"marks":1554,"value":1555,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Despite their potential, these technologies face challenges to widespread adoption. Schröder et al. report that METs struggle with performance, robustness, and cost once they leave the lab. When METs are scaled up to treat real wastewater, power and product yields fall; it is harder to keep microbes, electrodes, and water close together; and electrodes and separators can clog or foul.  ",{"data":1557,"content":1558,"nodeType":1133},{},[1559],{"data":1560,"marks":1561,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1563,"content":1564,"nodeType":1133},{},[1565],{"data":1566,"marks":1567,"value":1568,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"Designing systems that can cope with changing flows and need little maintenance is still more expensive than conventional equipment, so METs are rarely chosen as core treatment steps. ",{"data":1570,"content":1571,"nodeType":1133},{},[1572],{"data":1573,"marks":1574,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1576,"content":1577,"nodeType":1133},{},[1578],{"data":1579,"marks":1580,"value":1581,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"They also point to institutional barriers. ",{"data":1583,"content":1584,"nodeType":1133},{},[1585],{"data":1586,"marks":1587,"value":19,"nodeType":1124},{},[],{"data":1589,"content":1590,"nodeType":1133},{},[1591],{"data":1592,"marks":1593,"value":1594,"nodeType":1124},{},[],"The authors highlight that progress will depend on cheaper, longer-lived materials, more standardized modules, and long-term pilots in real plants—especially for niche and decentralized uses. treatment solutions Lead article Frontiers in Science Lead Article Published on 24 Feb 2026 Waste to value: microbial electrochemical technologies for sustainable water, material, and energy cycles Uwe Schröder Falk Harnisch Elizabeth Heidrich Ioannis A. Ieropoulos Bruce E. Logan Dibyojyoty Nath Deepak Pant Sunil A. Patil Sebastia Puig Jason Ren Ruggero Rossi Amelia-Elena Rotaru Annemiek ter Heijne Frontiers in Science doi 10.3389/fsci.2026.1688727 68,419 views 11 citations Expert insights ARTICLE EVENT Discussion with the article authors Prof Uwe Schröder (University of Greifswald, Germany), Prof Falk Harnisch (UFZ-Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, Germany), Prof Elizabeth Heidrich (Newcastle University, UK), and Dr Deepak Pant (Flemish Institute for Technological Research, Belgium) delved into next steps for circular wastewater treatment solutions. Watch now Frontiers in Science Editorial Published on 24 Feb 2026 From wastewater treatment to value recovery: the promise of microbial electrochemical technologies Prof Bruce E. Rittmann and Prof César I. Torres, Arizona State University, USA—Earliest impacts of microbial electrochemical technologies may emerge as infrastructure upgrades that boost digester performance and enable real-time monitoring and process control. Frontiers in Science Viewpoint Published on 18 Mar 2026 Advancing microbial electrochemical technologies for the circular economy, energy resilience, and environmental sustainability Prof Veera Gnaneswar Gude, Purdue University Northwest, USA—Microbial electrochemical technologies must evolve through optimized electron transfer, integrated treatment-resource recovery, and AI-informed design supporting nexus-based, circular economy applications beyond conventional wastewater treatment. POLICY OUTLOOK Published on 24 Feb 2026 Waste streams hold the key to water-related sustainable development Prof Manzoor Qadir, United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, Canada—Scaling wastewater systems for water security, nutrient reuse, and energy production requires fit-for-purpose regulation, trusted nutrient markets, public-private investment, and cross-sector policies. Key points Microbial electrochemical technologies (METs) present a transformative approach to wastewater treatment by simultaneously enabling energy recovery, clean water production, and nutrient recycling. Global wastewater could produce over 800,000 GWh of chemical energy annually, and this is currently largely untapped. The recovery of ammonia and phosphate using METs offers a compelling route to circular nutrient management and sustainable agriculture. Despite promising lab-scale results, METs face challenges in scalability, energy efficiency, and cost, with pilot-scale systems often underperforming due to increased resistance and complex wastewater matrices. Integrating METs with established treatment systems (e.g., anaerobic digestion or membrane bioreactors) and novel applications (e.g., hydroponics or remote sensors) extends their viability for both centralized and decentralized sanitation solutions. Field deployments in underserved regions demonstrate the potential of METs for low-cost, decentralized energy and sanitation infrastructure, addressing multiple Sustainable Development Goals. https://www.frontiersin.org/about/qualit.visible_text: Our approach to quality Skip to main content About us About us Who we are Mission and values History Leadership Awards Impact and progress Frontiers' impact Our annual reports Thought leadership Researcher perspectives Publishing model How we publish Open access Quality and research integrity Peer review Technology and platforms Research Topics Publish your data with FAIR² Fee policy Services Societies National consortia Institutional partnerships Collaboration and indexation More from Frontiers Frontiers Forum Frontiers Planet Prize Press office Sustainability Career opportunities Contact us All journals All articles Submit manuscript Submit data Search About us About us Who we are Mission and values History Leadership Awards Impact and progress Frontiers' impact Our annual reports Thought leadership Researcher perspectives Publishing model How we publish Open access Quality and research integrity Peer review Technology and platforms Research Topics Publish your data with FAIR² Fee policy Services Societies National consortia Institutional partnerships Collaboration and indexation More from Frontiers Frontiers Forum Frontiers Planet Prize Press office Sustainability Career opportunities Contact us All journals All articles Submit manuscript Submit data Quality and research integrity More than just a checkpoint: built by design into everything we do to safeguard academic research Our three-pronged approach to quality We take a unique, integrated approach to peer review and research integrity to deliver trusted science at scale. Our three mutually reinforcing pillars - combining dedicated research integrity teams, independent editorial boards, and responsible AI and technology - work together, continuously informing and strengthening one another. Our in-house teams Our research integrity and review teams are the first step in ensuring only high quality research makes it to peer review. Our editorial boards Frontiers’ editorial boards bring together leading scientists from the world’s top institutions, empowered to shape their fields and safeguard the quality of the research we publish. Our approach to AI Our AI platforms work alongside editors and research integrity specialists, enabling faster, smarter decisions and allowing us to scale quality without compromise. How we ensure quality across our journals Each manuscript submitted to Frontiers goes through our rigorous peer review process, supported by quality policies and checks before, during, and after publication. To safeguard the integrity of academic publishing, Frontiers is a member of major publishing regulatory and ethical committees. Publication policies and ethics Learn about our publishing policies, guidelines, and support for authors on ethical research conduct. Peer review Our unique peer review process provides a rigorous and transparent review by experts to ensure that only high quality articles are published. Collaboration and indexation Frontiers' journals are recognized in international indexes and repositories and we're accredited by major publishing regulatory and ethical committees including COPE. Our approach works – see the results of our commitment to quality The result is consistently high-quality publications with measurable impact, reflected in our citation rates and high ratings for quality from surveys conducted among the research community. By combining expertise, integrity, and innovation, we set a new standard for trust and excellence in open science. Our impact We measure our quality objectively, using industry-recognized metrics. Learn about the reach and influence of the research we publish. Researchers' perspectives Our dedication to quality and rigor delivers measurable results and we ask researchers in our community to hold us accountable. See our latest survey results. Our awards The quality of Frontiers' open access platform and our success as an open science pioneer has been recognized with numerous awards. Latest quality and research integrity news AI SUPPORT Published on 13 Apr 2026 Frontiers launches practical AI guidance for researchers Our AI playbook contains unique-in-publishing guidance covering the entire publication lifecycle – from researchers to editors and peer reviewers. AWARDS SUCCESS Published on 29 May 2026 Frontiers wins for pioneering work on AI in publishing Frontiers wins a gold award and a silver award at the 2026 EPIC Awards for a landmark whitepaper on AI in research and publishing, and a digital campaign making research integrity visible. ETHICS NEWS Published on 26 Mar 2026 Frontiers' ethics head elected COPE trustee Dr Marie Soulière, Frontiers' Head of Editorial Ethics and Quality Assurance, has been officially elected as a Trustee of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE). Sci., 24 February 2026</p><p class="LaySummary__infoText"> This explainer is part of an article hub, related to lead article <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fsci.2026.1688727" target="_self">https://doi.org/10.3389/fsci.2026.1688727</a></p></div><div class="Renderer"><!--[--><h1>How microbe-powered tech cleans and recovers value from wastewater</h1><p>The world generates about 359 billion m³ of wastewater each year, yet only ~52% is treated. Treatment is also energy-hungry—a growing issue as more places expand sanitation.  

</p><p>In their <a href="https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/science/articles/10.3389/fsci.2026.1688727/full">Frontiers in Science</a> article, Schröder et al. review microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)—where microbes help clean water while producing electricity or fuels and reclaiming valuable nutrients. They summarize what’s proven, what pilots show, and the key hurdles.</p><p></p><p>This explainer summarizes the article’s main points.</p><p></p><div class="FrontiersVideo__wrapper Renderer__entry--block"><div class="FrontiersVideo__container"><iframe class="FrontiersVideo__video" width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/aUqwolOSNg0?rel=0&autoplay=1&mute=1&controls=0&cc_load_policy=0&playlist=aUqwolOSNg0&loop=1" title="Video player" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen allow="autoplay"></iframe></div><!----></div><p></p><h2>What is wastewater? </h2><p>Wastewater is water that has been used and now carries substances we don’t want in the environment—mainly organic matter and nutrients, plus other contaminants. It refers to everyday sewage (toilets, showers, laundry), used industrial and commercial water (rinsing, cooling, cleaning), and food-related streams (kitchens, restaurants, food processing). </p><p></p><p>Treatment removes these substances to prevent pollution and protect drinking water sources. </p><p></p><h2>How much resource is in wastewater? </h2><p>Wastewater contains three main resource pools:  </p><ul><li><p><strong>energy:</strong> the organic matter in global wastewater holds over 800,000 GWh of energy each year</p></li><li><p><strong>fertilizer nutrients:</strong> around 14 million tons of nitrogen and about 3 million tons of phosphorus annually—equivalent to roughly 10–11% of global ammonia demand and around 7% of phosphate demand</p></li><li><p><strong>water: </strong>after treatment, wastewater becomes clean water for irrigation, construction, industrial cooling, landscaping, and groundwater recharge—With further treatment it can become potable.</p></li></ul><p></p><p>These resources are currently removed or discarded separately, often at high energy cost.  </p><p></p><h2>What are microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)? </h2><p>Reclaiming these lost resources from wastewater can support cleaner water with lower net energy demand than current approaches.  </p><p>

The authors discuss how METs—devices where special "electrogenic” bacteria move electrons to electrodes as they digest waste—can help us achieve this. </p><p>

The authors review two key types of MET:</p><ul><li><p><strong>microbial fuel cells (MFCs):</strong> these use electroactive microbes to oxidize organic matter at an anode and produce a small electrical current while the water is treated</p></li><li><p><strong>microbial electrolysis cells (MECs):</strong> these add some voltage so the cathode makes hydrogen (or sometimes methane) during treatment.</p></li></ul><p></p><h2>What have pilot studies shown outside the lab? </h2><p>Pilot projects show that METs can treat varying amounts of real wastewater. These range from tens of liters up to full-scale constructed wetlands, generally removing a substantial share of organics and nutrients. </p><p></p><p>Schröder et al. classify the following examples using technology readiness levels (TRLs)—a standard scale for how close a technology is to real-world use, from 1 (least ready) to 9 (most ready): </p><ul><li><p><strong>constructed wetlands with MET media (METland®) </strong>in Europe that clean municipal and industrial wastewater (TRL 7–8) </p></li><li><p><strong>MFC-based biosensors</strong> that monitor treatment performance and toxicity. Commercial systems use pre-loaded electrodes to give continuous signals linked to biological activity (TRL 6-9) </p></li><li><p><strong>modular MFC units for very concentrated industrial wastewater</strong>, which treat swine and beverage wastewaters continuously for months, removing organic pollution and generating some electricity (TRL 5-7) </p></li><li><p><strong>urine-focused MET stacks (Pee Power® and ammonia recovery)</strong> that have powered toilet lighting at the UK’s Glastonbury Festival and in field trials in Uganda, Kenya, and South Africa. Scaled-up MECs have also recovered ammonia and phosphorus from source-separated urine (TRL 5-6) </p></li><li><p><strong>MFCs for municipal wastewater</strong>—reactors of about 255–850 L that run for a year or more on real sewage. These operate reliably to remove a substantial amount of organic pollution, but produce far less electricity than equivalent lab systems (TRL 5-6) </p></li><li><p><strong>MECs for hydrogen and final treatment</strong>—reactors of about 100–1,000 L at treatment plants and industrial sites such as winery and hydrothermal liquefaction wastewaters. They combine the removal of organics and nitrogen with hydrogen recovery, but costs and long-term electrode performance limit their wider use (TRL 5-6) </p></li></ul><p></p><h2>Where do METs fit into existing infrastructure? </h2><p>In these scenarios, METs are added as extra steps in existing plants rather than replacing whole works. They are placed where wastewater is still relatively concentrated—early in the process or on side-streams from sludge handling and anaerobic digestion. This means they can recover organics and nutrients and reduce the load on later, more energy-intensive stages. </p><p></p><p>Some systems are built directly into existing units (for example, into beds, tanks, or filters) so they can provide both treatment and recovery in the same footprint. Related bioelectrochemical systems can also be used purely as sensors, sitting in pipes or tanks and sending continuous performance markers, without changing the main processes. </p><p></p><figure collection and sludge treatment, including key complementary technologies required for effective operation" loading="eager"></picture><!----></figure><p></p><h2>What are the current limits, and how can they be overcome? </h2><p>Despite their potential, these technologies face challenges to widespread adoption. Schröder et al. report that METs struggle with performance, robustness, and cost once they leave the lab. When METs are scaled up to treat real wastewater, power and product yields fall; it is harder to keep microbes, electrodes, and water close together; and electrodes and separators can clog or foul.  </p><p></p><p>Designing systems that can cope with changing flows and need little maintenance is still more expensive than conventional equipment, so METs are rarely chosen as core treatment steps. </p><p></p><p>They also point to institutional barriers. Utilities companies and regulators focus on meeting discharge limits at the lowest cost, while energy, hydrogen, or fertilizer recovered from wastewater often has uncertain value or legal status.  </p><p></p><p>The authors highlight that progress will depend on cheaper, longer-lived materials, more standardized modules, and long-term pilots in real plants—especially for niche and decentralized uses. </p><p></p><p>They argue that this will need to be combined with policies and business models that reward resource recovery alongside pollution control. </p><!--]--></div><div class="LaySummary__footer"><b>Republishing guidelines:</b> Open access and sharing research is part of <a href="/about/mission">Frontiers' mission</a>. cycles",["Date","2026-01-27T09:17:30.000Z"],["Date","2025-08-19T12:12:54.000Z"],["Date","2026-02-24T00:00:00.000Z"],["Date","2026-09-13T02:14:10.923Z"],"Global wastewater production exceeds 359 billion m3 annually, of which only 52% is treated, mostly in expensive and resource-consuming processes. Microbial electrochemical technologies (METs) offer a transformative approach to sustainable wastewater management by converting waste into valuable resources such as energy, clean water, and nutrients. They present a viable solution to the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 6 (to ensure access to water and sanitation for all) by enhancing both sanitation and resource recovery. METs, including microbial fuel cells (MFCs) and microbial electrolysis cells (MECs), harness electrogenic microorganisms to oxidize organic matter, generating electric energy or producing energy carriers like hydrogen and methane. METs also enable recovery of nutrients, such as ammonium and phosphates, which are essential for agriculture, thereby closing resource loops in a circular economy. Despite their potential, challenges remain in scaling up METs for widespread application. Pilot-scale MFCs and MECs have demonstrated feasibility, achieving up to 90% chemical oxygen demand removal and producing electric power, methane, or hydrogen from wastewater. However, high capital costs, material limitations, and energy efficiency barriers hinder commercialization. Innovations in electrode design, modular configurations, and integration with existing wastewater treatment processes (e.g., anaerobic digestion, membrane bioreactors, or constructed wetlands) are advancing METs toward higher technology readiness levels (TRLs 4–8). Field applications, like a system for urine-based electricity generation in underserved regions, highlight METs adaptability and societal impact. The transition from laboratory to real-world implementation requires scaling, process integration, and further optimization to reduce costs and improve performance. By aligning with circular economy principles, METs can transform wastewater into a resource, contributing to energy security, environmental sustainability, and global sanitation goals. ",{"data":1231,"content":1232,"nodeType":1136},{},[1233],{"data":1234,"marks":1235,"value":1236,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Wastewater contains three main resource pools:  ",{"data":1238,"content":1239,"nodeType":1287},{},[1240,1257,1272],{"data":1241,"content":1242,"nodeType":1256},{},[1243],{"data":1244,"content":1245,"nodeType":1136},{},[1246,1252],{"data":1247,"marks":1248,"value":1251,"nodeType":1127},{},[1249],{"type":1250},"bold","energy:",{"data":1253,"marks":1254,"value":1255,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," the organic matter in global wastewater holds over 800,000 GWh of energy each year","list-item",{"data":1258,"content":1259,"nodeType":1256},{},[1260],{"data":1261,"content":1262,"nodeType":1136},{},[1263,1268],{"data":1264,"marks":1265,"value":1267,"nodeType":1127},{},[1266],{"type":1250},"fertilizer nutrients:",{"data":1269,"marks":1270,"value":1271,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," around 14 million tons of nitrogen and about 3 million tons of phosphorus annually—equivalent to roughly 10–11% of global ammonia demand and around 7% of phosphate demand",{"data":1273,"content":1274,"nodeType":1256},{},[1275],{"data":1276,"content":1277,"nodeType":1136},{},[1278,1283],{"data":1279,"marks":1280,"value":1282,"nodeType":1127},{},[1281],{"type":1250},"water: ",{"data":1284,"marks":1285,"value":1286,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"after treatment, wastewater becomes clean water for irrigation, construction, industrial cooling, landscaping, and groundwater recharge—With further treatment it can become potable.","unordered-list",{"data":1289,"content":1290,"nodeType":1136},{},[1291],{"data":1292,"marks":1293,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1295,"content":1296,"nodeType":1136},{},[1297],{"data":1298,"marks":1299,"value":1300,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"These resources are currently removed or discarded separately, often at high energy cost.  ",{"data":1302,"content":1303,"nodeType":1136},{},[1304],{"data":1305,"marks":1306,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1308,"content":1309,"nodeType":1196},{},[1310],{"data":1311,"marks":1312,"value":1313,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"What are microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)? ",{"data":1315,"content":1316,"nodeType":1136},{},[1317],{"data":1318,"marks":1319,"value":1320,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Reclaiming these lost resources from wastewater can support cleaner water with lower net energy demand than current approaches.  ",{"data":1322,"content":1323,"nodeType":1136},{},[1324],{"data":1325,"marks":1326,"value":1327,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"\n\nThe authors discuss how METs—devices where special \"electrogenic” bacteria move electrons to electrodes as they digest waste—can help us achieve this. ",{"data":1329,"content":1330,"nodeType":1136},{},[1331],{"data":1332,"marks":1333,"value":1334,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"\n\nThe authors review two key types of MET:",{"data":1336,"content":1337,"nodeType":1287},{},[1338,1353],{"data":1339,"content":1340,"nodeType":1256},{},[1341],{"data":1342,"content":1343,"nodeType":1136},{},[1344,1349],{"data":1345,"marks":1346,"value":1348,"nodeType":1127},{},[1347],{"type":1250},"microbial fuel cells (MFCs):",{"data":1350,"marks":1351,"value":1352,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," these use electroactive microbes to oxidize organic matter at an anode and produce a small electrical current while the water is treated",{"data":1354,"content":1355,"nodeType":1256},{},[1356],{"data":1357,"content":1358,"nodeType":1136},{},[1359,1364],{"data":1360,"marks":1361,"value":1363,"nodeType":1127},{},[1362],{"type":1250},"microbial electrolysis cells (MECs):",{"data":1365,"marks":1366,"value":1367,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," these add some voltage so the cathode makes hydrogen (or sometimes methane) during treatment.",{"data":1369,"content":1370,"nodeType":1136},{},[1371],{"data":1372,"marks":1373,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1375,"content":1376,"nodeType":1196},{},[1377],{"data":1378,"marks":1379,"value":1380,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"What have pilot studies shown outside the lab? ",{"data":1382,"content":1383,"nodeType":1136},{},[1384],{"data":1385,"marks":1386,"value":1387,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Pilot projects show that METs can treat varying amounts of real wastewater. These range from tens of liters up to full-scale constructed wetlands, generally removing a substantial share of organics and nutrients. ",{"data":1389,"content":1390,"nodeType":1136},{},[1391],{"data":1392,"marks":1393,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1395,"content":1396,"nodeType":1136},{},[1397],{"data":1398,"marks":1399,"value":1400,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Schröder et al. classify the following examples using technology readiness levels (TRLs)—a standard scale for how close a technology is to real-world use, from 1 (least ready) to 9 (most ready): ",{"data":1402,"content":1403,"nodeType":1287},{},[1404,1419,1434,1449,1464,1479],{"data":1405,"content":1406,"nodeType":1256},{},[1407],{"data":1408,"content":1409,"nodeType":1136},{},[1410,1415],{"data":1411,"marks":1412,"value":1414,"nodeType":1127},{},[1413],{"type":1250},"constructed wetlands with MET media (METland®) ",{"data":1416,"marks":1417,"value":1418,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"in Europe that clean municipal and industrial wastewater (TRL 7–8) ",{"data":1420,"content":1421,"nodeType":1256},{},[1422],{"data":1423,"content":1424,"nodeType":1136},{},[1425,1430],{"data":1426,"marks":1427,"value":1429,"nodeType":1127},{},[1428],{"type":1250},"MFC-based biosensors",{"data":1431,"marks":1432,"value":1433,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," that monitor treatment performance and toxicity. Commercial systems use pre-loaded electrodes to give continuous signals linked to biological activity (TRL 6-9) ",{"data":1435,"content":1436,"nodeType":1256},{},[1437],{"data":1438,"content":1439,"nodeType":1136},{},[1440,1445],{"data":1441,"marks":1442,"value":1444,"nodeType":1127},{},[1443],{"type":1250},"modular MFC units for very concentrated industrial wastewater",{"data":1446,"marks":1447,"value":1448,"nodeType":1127},{},[],", which treat swine and beverage wastewaters continuously for months, removing organic pollution and generating some electricity (TRL 5-7) ",{"data":1450,"content":1451,"nodeType":1256},{},[1452],{"data":1453,"content":1454,"nodeType":1136},{},[1455,1460],{"data":1456,"marks":1457,"value":1459,"nodeType":1127},{},[1458],{"type":1250},"urine-focused MET stacks (Pee Power® and ammonia recovery)",{"data":1461,"marks":1462,"value":1463,"nodeType":1127},{},[]," that have powered toilet lighting at the UK’s Glastonbury Festival and in field trials in Uganda, Kenya, and South Africa. Scaled-up MECs have also recovered ammonia and phosphorus from source-separated urine (TRL 5-6) ",{"data":1465,"content":1466,"nodeType":1256},{},[1467],{"data":1468,"content":1469,"nodeType":1136},{},[1470,1475],{"data":1471,"marks":1472,"value":1474,"nodeType":1127},{},[1473],{"type":1250},"MFCs for municipal wastewater",{"data":1476,"marks":1477,"value":1478,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"—reactors of about 255–850 L that run for a year or more on real sewage. These operate reliably to remove a substantial amount of organic pollution, but produce far less electricity than equivalent lab systems (TRL 5-6) ",{"data":1480,"content":1481,"nodeType":1256},{},[1482],{"data":1483,"content":1484,"nodeType":1136},{},[1485,1490],{"data":1486,"marks":1487,"value":1489,"nodeType":1127},{},[1488],{"type":1250},"MECs for hydrogen and final treatment",{"data":1491,"marks":1492,"value":1493,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"—reactors of about 100–1,000 L at treatment plants and industrial sites such as winery and hydrothermal liquefaction wastewaters. They combine the removal of organics and nitrogen with hydrogen recovery, but costs and long-term electrode performance limit their wider use (TRL 5-6) ",{"data":1495,"content":1496,"nodeType":1136},{},[1497],{"data":1498,"marks":1499,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1501,"content":1502,"nodeType":1196},{},[1503],{"data":1504,"marks":1505,"value":1506,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Where do METs fit into existing infrastructure? ",{"data":1508,"content":1509,"nodeType":1136},{},[1510],{"data":1511,"marks":1512,"value":1513,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"In these scenarios, METs are added as extra steps in existing plants rather than replacing whole works. They are placed where wastewater is still relatively concentrated—early in the process or on side-streams from sludge handling and anaerobic digestion. This means they can recover organics and nutrients and reduce the load on later, more energy-intensive stages. ",{"data":1515,"content":1516,"nodeType":1136},{},[1517],{"data":1518,"marks":1519,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1521,"content":1522,"nodeType":1136},{},[1523],{"data":1524,"marks":1525,"value":1526,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Some systems are built directly into existing units (for example, into beds, tanks, or filters) so they can provide both treatment and recovery in the same footprint. Related bioelectrochemical systems can also be used purely as sensors, sitting in pipes or tanks and sending continuous performance markers, without changing the main processes. ",{"data":1528,"content":1529,"nodeType":1136},{},[1530],{"data":1531,"marks":1532,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1534,"content":1538,"nodeType":1182},{"target":1535},{"sys":1536},{"id":1537,"type":254,"linkType":1180},"ax9galbI1WWuPGgrwNcfC",[],{"data":1540,"content":1541,"nodeType":1136},{},[1542],{"data":1543,"marks":1544,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1546,"content":1547,"nodeType":1196},{},[1548],{"data":1549,"marks":1550,"value":1551,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"What are the current limits, and how can they be overcome? ",{"data":1553,"content":1554,"nodeType":1136},{},[1555],{"data":1556,"marks":1557,"value":1558,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Despite their potential, these technologies face challenges to widespread adoption. Schröder et al. report that METs struggle with performance, robustness, and cost once they leave the lab. When METs are scaled up to treat real wastewater, power and product yields fall; it is harder to keep microbes, electrodes, and water close together; and electrodes and separators can clog or foul.  ",{"data":1560,"content":1561,"nodeType":1136},{},[1562],{"data":1563,"marks":1564,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1566,"content":1567,"nodeType":1136},{},[1568],{"data":1569,"marks":1570,"value":1571,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"Designing systems that can cope with changing flows and need little maintenance is still more expensive than conventional equipment, so METs are rarely chosen as core treatment steps. ",{"data":1573,"content":1574,"nodeType":1136},{},[1575],{"data":1576,"marks":1577,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1579,"content":1580,"nodeType":1136},{},[1581],{"data":1582,"marks":1583,"value":1584,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"They also point to institutional barriers. Utilities companies and regulators focus on meeting discharge limits at the lowest cost, while energy, hydrogen, or fertilizer recovered from wastewater often has uncertain value or legal status.  ",{"data":1586,"content":1587,"nodeType":1136},{},[1588],{"data":1589,"marks":1590,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1592,"content":1593,"nodeType":1136},{},[1594],{"data":1595,"marks":1596,"value":1597,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"The authors highlight that progress will depend on cheaper, longer-lived materials, more standardized modules, and long-term pilots in real plants—especially for niche and decentralized uses. ",{"data":1599,"content":1600,"nodeType":1136},{},[1601],{"data":1602,"marks":1603,"value":19,"nodeType":1127},{},[],{"data":1605,"content":1606,"nodeType":1136},{},[1607],{"data":1608,"marks":1609,"value":1610,"nodeType":1127},{},[],"They argue that this will need to be combined with policies and business models that reward resource recovery alongside pollution control. Sci., 24 February 2026 This explainer is part of an article hub, related to lead article https://doi.org/10.3389/fsci.2026.1688727 How microbe-powered tech cleans and recovers value from wastewater The world generates about 359 billion m³ of wastewater each year, yet only ~52% is treated. Treatment is also energy-hungry—a growing issue as more places expand sanitation. In their Frontiers in Science article, Schröder et al. review microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)—where microbes help clean water while producing electricity or fuels and reclaiming valuable nutrients. They summarize what’s proven, what pilots show, and the key hurdles. This explainer summarizes the article’s main points. What is wastewater? Wastewater is water that has been used and now carries substances we don’t want in the environment—mainly organic matter and nutrients, plus other contaminants. It refers to everyday sewage (toilets, showers, laundry), used industrial and commercial water (rinsing, cooling, cleaning), and food-related streams (kitchens, restaurants, food processing). Treatment removes these substances to prevent pollution and protect drinking water sources. How much resource is in wastewater? Wastewater contains three main resource pools: energy: the organic matter in global wastewater holds over 800,000 GWh of energy each year fertilizer nutrients: around 14 million tons of nitrogen and about 3 million tons of phosphorus annually—equivalent to roughly 10–11% of global ammonia demand and around 7% of phosphate demand water: after treatment, wastewater becomes clean water for irrigation, construction, industrial cooling, landscaping, and groundwater recharge—With further treatment it can become potable. These resources are currently removed or discarded separately, often at high energy cost. What are microbial electrochemical technologies (METs)? Reclaiming these lost resources from wastewater can support cleaner water with lower net energy demand than current approaches. The authors discuss how METs—devices where special "electrogenic” bacteria move electrons to electrodes as they digest waste—can help us achieve this. The authors review two key types of MET: microbial fuel cells (MFCs): these use electroactive microbes to oxidize organic matter at an anode and produce a small electrical current while the water is treated microbial electrolysis cells (MECs): these add some voltage so the cathode makes hydrogen (or sometimes methane) during treatment. What have pilot studies shown outside the lab? Pilot projects show that METs can treat varying amounts of real wastewater. These range from tens of liters up to full-scale constructed wetlands, generally removing a substantial share of organics and nutrients. Schröder et al. classify the following examples using technology readiness levels (TRLs)—a standard scale for how close a technology is to real-world use, from 1 (least ready) to 9 (most ready): constructed wetlands with MET media (METland®) in Europe that clean municipal and industrial wastewater (TRL 7–8) MFC-based biosensors that monitor treatment performance and toxicity. Commercial systems use pre-loaded electrodes to give continuous signals linked to biological activity (TRL 6-9) modular MFC units for very concentrated industrial wastewater , which treat swine and beverage wastewaters continuously for months, removing organic pollution and generating some electricity (TRL 5-7) urine-focused MET stacks (Pee Power® and ammonia recovery) that have powered toilet lighting at the UK’s Glastonbury Festival and in field trials in Uganda, Kenya, and South Africa. Scaled-up MECs have also recovered ammonia and phosphorus from source-separated urine (TRL 5-6) MFCs for municipal wastewater —reactors of about 255–850 L that run for a year or more on real sewage. These operate reliably to remove a substantial amount of organic pollution, but produce far less electricity than equivalent lab systems (TRL 5-6) MECs for hydrogen and final treatment —reactors of about 100–1,000 L at treatment plants and industrial sites such as winery and hydrothermal liquefaction wastewaters. They combine the removal of organics and nitrogen with hydrogen recovery, but costs and long-term electrode performance limit their wider use (TRL 5-6) Where do METs fit into existing infrastructure? In these scenarios, METs are added as extra steps in existing plants rather than replacing whole works. They are placed where wastewater is still relatively concentrated—early in the process or on side-streams from sludge handling and anaerobic digestion. This means they can recover organics and nutrients and reduce the load on later, more energy-intensive stages. Some systems are built directly into existing units (for example, into beds, tanks, or filters) so they can provide both treatment and recovery in the same footprint. Related bioelectrochemical systems can also be used purely as sensors, sitting in pipes or tanks and sending continuous performance markers, without changing the main processes. What are the current limits, and how can they be overcome? Despite their potential, these technologies face challenges to widespread adoption. Schröder et al. report that METs struggle with performance, robustness, and cost once they leave the lab. When METs are scaled up to treat real wastewater, power and product yields fall; it is harder to keep microbes, electrodes, and water close together; and electrodes and separators can clog or foul. Designing systems that can cope with changing flows and need little maintenance is still more expensive than conventional equipment, so METs are rarely chosen as core treatment steps. They also point to institutional barriers. Utilities companies and regulators focus on meeting discharge limits at the lowest cost, while energy, hydrogen, or fertilizer recovered from wastewater often has uncertain value or legal status. The authors highlight that progress will depend on cheaper, longer-lived materials, more standardized modules, and long-term pilots in real plants—especially for niche and decentralized uses. They argue that this will need to be combined with policies and business models that reward resource recovery alongside pollution control.
